messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night the flood came, Elena had been awake, listening to the rain hammer against her apartment windows. She was a physical therapist then, as she is now, living in a ground-floor unit in a Houston suburb. The water did not rise slowly. It surged through the walls, through the door seams, carrying mud and debris. She had to climb onto her kitchen counter, then onto the refrigerator, her phone already dead, the current black and oily below her. She remembers the smell—wet earth, gasoline, rot—and the sound of things knocking against the walls in the dark. She was rescued by a neighbor in a boat just before dawn, but something in her had already been washed away.

In the weeks that followed, Elena found she could not look at a glass of water without her stomach turning. The nausea would rise first—a sudden, slick queasiness that had no clear cause—and then the memory would arrive, not as a full picture but as a wave of dread and cold, the feeling of the water rising against her ribs. She had come to believe that the memory did not belong to her. It felt like a film she had once watched, a story about someone else, yet the grief it carried was hers alone, heavy and inexplicable. Sometimes she would be standing in the grocery aisle and the grief would hit her without any image at all, just a crushing weight that made her want to sit down on the floor. She began to dwell on who she used to be—the woman who could sleep through a thunderstorm, who did not flinch at a sudden noise, who felt safe in her own home.

Elena now lives in a third-floor apartment in a different part of the city, but she has not truly settled. She only feels safe in a very limited number of places: her bedroom, the small coffee shop two blocks away where the barista knows her name, and the quiet corner of the clinic where she works. Anywhere else, her body stays on high alert. A car backfiring, a door slamming, the clatter of a dropped tray in the clinic cafeteria—each sound makes her jump, her heart hammering, her attention narrowing to a single point of threat. This constant vigilance has worn her down. She has trouble falling asleep, and when she does, she wakes at the slightest creak of the building, certain the water is coming back.

The safest place is her bedroom, and she has learned to stay there. She avoids going out unless she has to. She tells herself it is practical—there is nothing she needs—but the truth is that every outing carries risk. A patient in the clinic mentioning a vacation to the lake, the name "Houston" spoken on the television in the waiting room, the sound of a toilet flushing in the next stall—any of these can trigger the nausea, and the nausea brings the memory, and the memory brings the grief, and then she is gone. She has learned to leave her body deliberately, to blank out when the feeling becomes too much. She will stare at a spot on the wall until her mind goes white, and when she comes back, she is disoriented, sometimes tearful, and the memory feels even more alien than before. This dissociation, in turn, makes the triggers harder to resist. The next time she hears a name that reminds her of the flood, the nausea comes faster, and the cycle tightens.

At work, Elena is professional and competent. She guides her patients through their exercises with patience, her hands steady. But she has stopped taking lunch breaks in the staff lounge because someone left a news article about hurricane season on the table. She has stopped going to the clinic’s monthly team meetings because they are held in a basement room. Her supervisor has noticed her absences and has asked if everything is all right. Elena said yes, but she knows she is not all right. What finally brought her to seek help was a Tuesday morning in July, when a summer thunderstorm rolled in and the sky turned green. She felt the nausea, then the alien memory, then the grief, and she realized she had been standing in her patient’s room, frozen, a towel in her hand, unable to move or speak for nearly a minute. She is afraid of losing her job. She is afraid of never feeling like herself again. But what frightens her most is the thought that the water is still rising, and that no amount of staying home will keep it out.
